newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wants facts before S.Africa decision.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants facts before S.Africa decision.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it would not make a decision on possibly reducing aid to South Africa until it acquired more facts on Pretoria's plans to sell arms to Syria.

"The United States government is not going to make any decision and cannot make a decision on this issue until we get all the facts from the South African government," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

"I would suggest that we do that amicably and cooperatively in the tradition that we've established with the (Nelson) Mandela government over the past couple of years and that's how you'll see us talk about this issue," he said.

Washington on Monday warned it might be forced to cut U.S. aid to South Africa, which in 1997 totals $120 million, if Pretoria follows through with reported plans to sell Syria three billion rand ($641 million) in tank-gun aiming gear.
"We are deeply concerned about these reports. It would be extremely serious if these sales actually occurred," Burns told a news briefing at that time.

"The United States hopes that the South African government will not consummate arms sales to a country that supports terrorists," he said, referring to charges that have landed Syria on the U.S. list of terrorism-sponsoring nations that also includes Iran, Iraq, North Korea and Sudan.

In response, Mandela's spokesman Parks Mankahlana accused Washington of high-handed bullying, telling Reuters on Tuesday: "We detest this kind of behaviour ... We just don't like being shouted at...We'd rather be spoken to differently, as equals, instead of (Washington) making public threats."
A statement from South Africa's department of foreign affairs issued late in the day after a high-level meeting of ministry officials took a more conciliatory line.

In Pretoria's first full official statement on the deal, it said a local company "was involved in a process of marketing an electronic tank sighting system in Syria" along with companies from at least three European countries.
"It is expected that any tender for the sale of such equipment would be issued between the years 1999 and 2000," the statement said.
Asked to react to Mankahlana's charges, Burns gave a tempered response at Tuesday's briefing.

"I haven't seen those remarks. But I can just say we have a very good relationship with the government of South Africa and I'm sure that will continue, because our heads of state have a good personal relationship and we've been able to do a lot of business with South Africa. We want to continue that," he said.
"No one's putting a gun to anyone's head. And we intend to work with the South African government amicably, and cooperatively on this."
Burns reiterated that U.S. law could force a cut in aid to South Africa if the Syria deal goes through.
But he stressed that Washington does not yet "have all the facts, and that, obviously we're going be talking to the South African government before anything happens here."
